entry: Systematic method of representing the curved surface of a [[Globe|globe]] on a flat plane. Every projection of a sphere onto a plane distorts the surface in some way, so each one preserves some properties, such as area, shape, direction or distance, at the expense of others. The purpose of the map determines which projection suits it, and the study of projections centers on characterizing their distortions. The best-known is the [[Mercator projection]], which preserves angles but enlarges regions far from the equator; it was criticized through the 20th century and revived in the 21st for online mapping. Equal-area projections, such as the Gall–Peters projection, show the correct sizes of countries relative to one another but distort angles. In September 2026 the [[United Nations]] resolved to promote equal-area projections, notably the Equal Earth projection; 164 countries voted in favor, the [[United States]] voted against, and six abstained.

Genus of trees and shrubs in the soapberry family Sapindaceae, commonly known as maples. It contains approximately 132 species, most native to [[East Asia]], with others in Europe, northern Africa and [[North America]]. Most species are trees growing 10 to 45 m (33 to 148 ft) tall, while others are shrubs less than 10 m tall. Most species have palmate [[Leaf|leaves]], though a few exceptions exist, and all share distinctive winged [[Fruit|fruits]]. Maples are distinguished by their opposite leaf arrangement, and most species are deciduous. Many are grown in gardens for their [[Autumn|autumn]] color and decorative foliage. Maple syrup is made from the sap of some species. The closest relative of the maples is the small east Asian genus Dipteronia.

Indigenous people of south-central [[Chile]] and southwestern [[Argentina]], including parts of [[Patagonia]]. Also known as Araucanians, they share a common social, religious and economic structure and the Mapudungun language. Traditional life centered on agriculture, and their material culture is known for [[Textile|textiles]] and silverwork. Mapuche society in Araucanía and Patagonia remained independent until the late 19th century, when Chile occupied Araucanía and Argentina conquered the Puelmapu. Today the Mapuche make up 77.16% of Chile's Indigenous peoples, and many communities are engaged in the Mapuche conflict over land and Indigenous rights.

Capital and largest city of [[Mozambique]] (pop., 2017: 1,088,449). It lies on a large natural bay of the [[Indian Ocean]], within 120 kilometres of the borders with Eswatini and [[South Africa]]. It is a [[Port|port]] city with an economy centered on commerce, and its chief exports include cotton, sugar, chromite, sisal, copra and hardwood. The area was first settled by ancestral Tsonga people as a fishing village and was named Lourenço Marques, after a navigator who explored it in 1544; the name was used until 1976. Known as the City of Acacias and the Pearl of the Indian Ocean, Maputo has architecture that mixes Portuguese colonial styles with [[Art Deco|art deco]], [[Bauhaus]] and Brutalist buildings. Eduardo Mondlane University, the oldest in the country, is located there.

City and municipality in northwestern [[Venezuela]], capital of Zulia state (pop., 2019: 1,752,602). It is the second-largest city proper in Venezuela, after [[Caracas]], and is considered the economic center of western Venezuela because of the [[Petroleum|petroleum]] industry along the shores of [[Lake Maracaibo]]. The city was founded in 1574 as Nueva Zamora de la Laguna de Maracaibo, after two earlier attempts. It became a key transshipment point for inland settlements after pirates destroyed Gibraltar, at the head of the lake, in 1669. The discovery of petroleum in 1917 led to rapid population growth. It is sometimes called the First City of Venezuela for being the first to adopt various public services, including electricity.

Large coastal island in the Brazilian state of Pará, at the mouth of the [[Amazon River|Amazon]]. It is the main island of the Marajó Archipelago, the second-largest island in [[South America]] and the 35th largest in the world. Its land area of 40,100 square kilometres (15,500 mi2) is comparable to [[Switzerland]]. The island was the site of the Marajoara culture, which lasted from about 400 BC to 1600 AD and may have numbered more than 100,000 people at its peak. It is known today for its [[Water buffalo|water buffalo]], which number about 450,000, and for the pororoca, a tidal bore whose waves reach 4 m (13 ft) and attract [[Surfing|surfers]]. Much of the island floods in the rainy season, and its rivers are the principal means of transport.

Early modern confederacy in the Indian subcontinent, founded in 1674 under [[Shivaji]] and largely destroyed by 1818. For most of its existence it comprised the realms of the Peshwa, the hereditary prime minister based at Poona (now [[Pune]]), and four major Maratha states: the Scindia, Gaekwad, Holkar and Bhonsle families. Shivaji revolted against the Bijapur Sultanate and the [[Mughal Empire]], and under Peshwa Bajirao I the Maratha realm expanded into northern and central India. Defeat at Panipat in 1761 halted the expansion, though most lost territory was regained under Peshwa Madhavrao I. The confederacy was broken after the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha Wars, in which the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] intervened. Historians debate whether empire or confederacy is the right term, since power among its leaders often shifted.

[[Indo-Aryan languages|Indo-Aryan]] language of India, spoken mainly in the state of [[Maharashtra]]. Derived from Maharashtri Prakrit, it is the official language of Maharashtra and an additional official language in [[Goa]]. It is one of the 22 scheduled languages of India, with 83 million speakers as of the 2011 census. Marathi ranks third among Indian languages by number of native speakers, after Hindustani (Hindi-Urdu) and Bengali, and 15th in the world. It is written in [[Devanagari]] and has some of the oldest literature of any modern Indian language. It was probably first attested in a 739 CE copper-plate inscription from Satara. The [[Government of India|Government of India]] designated it a classical language in October 2024. Marathi has three genders: masculine, feminine and neuter.

Long-distance foot race of 42.195 kilometres (c. 26.22 mi), usually run as a road race, though the distance can also be covered on trails. It was one of the original events of the modern [[Olympic Games]], first held in 1896 in [[Athens]], and the distance was not standardized until 1921. It is included in the World Athletics Championships, which began in 1983, and is the only running road race in both championships. More than 800 marathons are held worldwide each year, mostly by recreational athletes. The name derives from a legend of the Greek messenger Pheidippides, said to have run from the [[Battle of Marathon|Battle of Marathon]] to Athens in 490 BC to announce victory, then died. Historians dispute the account, since the earliest source, [[Herodotus]], describes a run from Athens to [[Sparta]] and makes no mention of this one.

[[Metamorphic rock]] of recrystallized carbonate minerals, most commonly [[Calcite|calcite]] or dolomite. It forms when [[Limestone|limestone]] or dolomite is subjected to heat and pressure, and it has a crystalline texture and is typically not layered. Pure white marble results from very clean limestone or dolomite; its characteristic veins and swirls come from impurities such as clay, sand, iron oxides or [[Chert|chert]] in the original rock. Its hardness, durability and polishable surface make it valued in sculpture and architecture, and sculptors prize its uniform grain for fine detail. Marble is extracted by [[Quarry|quarrying]]. Production is dominated by China, Italy, India and Spain, which together account for almost half of world production of marble and decorative stone. Outdoor marble is damaged by [[Acid rain|acid rain]].

Small spherical toy, often made of glass, clay, steel, plastic or [[Agate|agate]]. Marbles are usually 0.5 to 3.5 cm (0.2 to 1.4 in) in diameter and are used in games, in marble runs and races, or as art objects. Collectors value them for their colors. Small stone balls from about 2500 BCE, found near [[Mohenjo-daro]] in the Indus Valley Civilization, are identified as marbles. Many examples come from sites associated with Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt. Marbles arrived in Britain from the Low Countries in the medieval era. In 1503 the town council of [[Nuremberg]] limited marble games to a meadow outside town, and the name marble, for balls once made of polished stone, dates from this era. Ceramic marbles entered inexpensive mass production in the 1870s. The British and World Marbles Championship has been held at Tinsley Green, West Sussex, every year since 1932.

American businessman, venture capitalist and former software engineer. He co-authored Mosaic, the first [[Web browser|web browser]] to display inline images, and co-founded Netscape. He co-founded the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, based in [[Silicon Valley]], and the social networking platform Ning. He sold the software company Opsware to [[Hewlett-Packard]]. In 2024 he became an advisor to [[Donald Trump]]. As of November 2026, [[Forbes]] estimated his net worth at US$18.5 billion.

Stage name of Marco Antonio Muñiz, American singer and actor. The top-selling [[Salsa music|salsa]] artist of all time, he had sold more than 12 million albums worldwide as of 2014. He has won four [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], eight Latin Grammy Awards and 29 Lo Nuestro Awards, and holds a Guinness World Record for best-selling tropical/salsa artist. He began as a session vocalist for freestyle and New York house acts, and his salsa style borrowed from [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]] and house. He appeared opposite [[Denzel Washington]] in *Man on Fire* (2004).

Russian and French artist of Jewish ancestry and an early modernist. Born into a Jewish family near Vitebsk, in what is now [[Belarus]], he worked in painting, stained glass, stage sets, ceramics and tapestries. His style blended [[Cubism|Cubism]], Symbolism and Fauvism with Eastern European and Jewish folklore. He left for Paris in 1923 and, during [[World War II|World War II]], escaped occupied France to the United States, where he lived in [[New York City]] for seven years before returning to France in 1948. His commissions include stained-glass windows for the cathedrals of Reims and Metz, windows for the United Nations, and part of the ceiling of the Paris Opéra. Art critic Robert Hughes called him the quintessential Jewish artist of the twentieth century.

American stand-up comedian, actor and former radio presenter and podcaster. From 2009 he hosted the twice-weekly [[Podcast|podcast]] WTF with Marc Maron, recorded in his garage in Highland Park, Los Angeles, and interviewed guests including [[Robin Williams]] and [[Barack Obama]]. The podcast ended in 2025 with Obama as its final guest. He starred in the IFC series *Maron* from 2013 to 2016 and co-starred in the [[Netflix]] series *GLOW* from 2017 to 2019. He appeared more than forty times on *Late Night with Conan O'Brien* in the 1990s and 2000s.

French-American artist, chess player and inventor, a key figure in the avant-garde. He is best known for [[Fountain (Duchamp)|Fountain]] (1917), an anti-art work in which he signed the name R. Mutt 1917 on a urinal. Duchamp spent the last 25 years of his life in New York City. Commonly regarded, along with [[Pablo Picasso]] and Georges Braque, as one of three artists who established the post-industrial perspective in art history, he is considered the progenitor of [[Conceptual art|conceptual art]]. His definition of the art coefficient influenced appropriation artists such as [[Andy Warhol]]. During his military service from 1905 he learned typography and printing processes, skills he later used in his work.

French [[Mime artist|mime artist]] and actor, most famous for his stage persona, Bip the Clown. He called mime the art of silence and performed professionally worldwide for more than 60 years. Born Marcel Mangel in Strasbourg to a Jewish family, he took the surname Marceau during the German occupation of France, in tribute to a general of the [[French Revolution]]. During World War II he and his brother joined the French Resistance in Limoges and helped rescue Jewish children. His father was captured by the Gestapo and killed at [[Auschwitz concentration camp|Auschwitz]]. Marceau created Bip in 1947, a clown in a striped pullover and battered opera hat whose misadventures made him his alter ego, as the Little Tramp was for [[Charlie Chaplin]].

French sociologist and anthropologist, known as the father of French ethnology. A nephew of [[Émile Durkheim]], he crossed the boundaries between sociology and anthropology. He is best known for his analyses of magic, [[Sacrifice|sacrifice]] and gift exchange in *The Gift* (1925), and he had a significant influence on [[Claude Lévi-Strauss]], the founder of structural anthropology. He studied linguistics, Sanskrit and the history of religions, and passed the agrégation in 1893. In 1901 he was appointed to the chair of the history of religions of non-civilized peoples at the École pratique des hautes études. He founded research institutions, including the Institut d'Ethnologie in 1926, which stimulated fieldwork-based anthropology among young academics.

French novelist, literary critic and essayist, best known for *In Search of Lost Time*. Published in seven volumes between 1913 and 1927, the novel totals around 1.25 million words, and critics and writers consider it one of the most influential works of the twentieth century. Its themes include desire, artistic creativity, sexuality and class, and it helped pioneer the stream of consciousness technique. Proust was born in [[Paris]] to a wealthy [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeois]] family; his father, Adrien Proust, was a prominent pathologist who studied [[Cholera|cholera]]. Severe [[Asthma|asthma]] attacks from childhood disrupted his education, and illness confined him during the last three years of his life. He died of [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] in 1922, and his brother Robert published the remaining volumes posthumously.

Italian actor, regarded as one of Italy's most iconic male performers of the 20th century. He appeared in 147 films between 1939 and 1996 and played leading roles for many of the country's top directors. He became an international celebrity through his films with [[Federico Fellini]], including *La Dolce Vita* (1960) and *8½* (1963). He formed a notable on-screen partnership with [[Sophia Loren]], co-starring with her in eleven films. He was the first actor to receive an Academy Award nomination for a non-English-language performance, and he was nominated for Best Actor three times, for *Divorce Italian Style*, *A Special Day* and *Dark Eyes*. He largely shunned Hollywood.

American actress who won an Academy Award for playing artist Lee Krasner in *Pollock* (2000). Her breakthrough came in 1990 with the [[Coen brothers|Coen brothers]]' film *Miller's Crossing*. She was also nominated for an Academy Award for *Mystic River* (2003). On Broadway she was nominated for a Tony Award for *Angels in America* and won one for *God of Carnage* (2009). Her television credits include the [[HBO]] series *The Newsroom* and the [[CBS]] series *Code Black*.

British chef, restaurateur and television personality. In 1995 he became the first British chef to earn three Michelin stars and, at age 33, the youngest chef to do so. He opened Harveys in Wandsworth Common, London, in 1987, and won his first star almost immediately. He trained chefs including [[Gordon Ramsay]], and he has been dubbed the first celebrity chef. He left school without qualifications, and after realizing he was dyslexic when his son was diagnosed, he taught himself to read and spell.

Venetian merchant, explorer and writer, known for an account of travels in Asia. He traveled the [[Silk Road|Silk Road]] between 1271 and 1295 and reached the court of [[Kublai Khan]], who appointed him an emissary. He undertook diplomatic missions across the empire and Southeast Asia, to present-day Myanmar, India, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Vietnam, and he lived in China for 17 years. After returning to Venice, he was captured in the war between Venice and [[Genoa]]. While imprisoned, he dictated his travels to Rustichello da Pisa, producing *The Travels of Marco Polo* (c. 1300). The book gave Europeans a detailed view of China, Persia and India, and was the first Western record of [[Porcelain|porcelain]], gunpowder and [[Paper money|paper money]]. Its narrative inspired [[Christopher Columbus]].

Dutch former football player and manager, a striker for Ajax, [[AC Milan|AC Milan]] and the Netherlands national team. He scored more than 300 goals at club and international level. He won the Ballon d'Or three times and was named [[FIFA|FIFA]] World Player of the Year in 1992. At UEFA Euro 1988 he won the Golden Boot with five goals, including a volley in the final against the Soviet Union. A recurring ankle injury ended his career, with his last game at age 28 and retirement at 30. He later coached Ajax and the Netherlands.

Roman emperor (r. 161–180) and Stoic philosopher. He was the last of the so-called Five Good Emperors and the last emperor of the Pax Romana, an age of relative peace in the [[Roman Empire|Roman Empire]] lasting from 27 BC to 180 AD. He ruled jointly with Lucius Verus until Verus died in 169, and he was succeeded by his son [[Commodus]]. His reign was marked by the Parthian War and the Marcomannic Wars against the Marcomanni, Quadi and Iazyges. The Antonine Plague, which broke out in 165 or 166, caused the deaths of five to ten million people. His *Meditations*, private reflections written in Greek, is one of the most important sources for understanding ancient Stoic philosophy.
